title: Comics of the New Europe
abstract: Bringing together the work of an array of North American and European scholars, this collection highlights a previously unexamined area within global comics studies. It analyses comics from countries formerly behind the Iron Curtain like East Germany, Poland, Czech Republic, Hungary, Romania, Yugoslavia, and Ukraine, given their shared history of WWII and communism. In addition to situating these graphic narratives in their national and subnational contexts, Comics of the New Europe pays particular attention to transnational connections along the common themes of nostalgia, memoir, and life under communism. The essays offer insights into a new generation of European cartoonists that looks forward, inspired and informed by traditions from Franco-Belgian and American comics, and back, as they use the medium of comics to reexamine and reevaluate not only their national pasts and respective comics traditions but also their own post-1989 identities and experiences.

Comics of the New Europe shows early signs of real use and reach: it has been downloaded 2,249 times, appears to have informed two recorded discussions, and was supported through Knowledge Unlatched. Full narrative

Comics of the New Europe is a 2023 scholarly volume from Leuven University Press that brings comics studies into conversation with the political and cultural histories of post–Iron Curtain Europe. Its conceptual profile centers on comics, memoir, communism, history, and narrative, reflecting the book’s focus on graphic narratives from countries such as East Germany, Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Romania, Yugoslavia, and Ukraine. The volume is openly available in a hybrid model, which helps explain its visible usage.

The clearest impact signal in the record is sustained readership. OAPEN reports 2,249 downloads, indicating active use beyond an initial publication burst. That pattern suggests the book is being sought out by readers with interest in comics scholarship, cultural history, and area studies, although download data should be read as evidence of access and attention rather than citation-based scholarly influence.

There is also some indication of teaching or educational uptake. The book is discussed in two recorded YouTube videos, one from NYU’s Jordan Center and one from the Czech Literary Centre. These references do not establish formal syllabus adoption, but they do show that the volume has entered public scholarly and cultural discussion in ways that can support teaching, outreach, and specialist conversation.

The citation record is still early. OpenAlex currently shows no citations, so there is not yet a citation-based signal of academic accumulation. In a book of this kind, that is not unusual soon after publication; the available evidence instead points to circulation, discoverability, and use. Funding support from Knowledge Unlatched further aligns the book with open-access dissemination, which likely contributes to its download performance.

Overall, the record portrays a book with clear readership and some educational visibility, but limited formal scholarly citation uptake so far. Its strongest impact lies in making an underexamined area of comics scholarship more accessible and usable across research and teaching contexts.
